questions.question: What is a mixture distribution?
options: A distribution with exactly one possible value
A distribution that ignores conditional probabilities, under all circumstances whatsoever.
A distribution obtained by averaging conditional distributions using probabilities of a random index
A PMF whose masses sum to two

questions.question: What does a mixture distribution combine?
What do mixture weights have to satisfy?
options: They are negative and sum to zero
They are nonnegative and sum to one

questions.question: What kind of population situation does a mixture represent?
options: A population made of different hidden groups
A sample space with no outcomes

questions.question: What shape can mixtures produce even when each component is unimodal?
Customer spending modeled from business and leisure customers is an example of what?
Machine lifetime from old and new machines can form what?
options: A CDF with total probability zero
A random variable with no support

questions.question: Exam scores from two preparation groups can form what kind of distribution?
options: A support outside the real line

questions.question: If mixture weights are $0.3$ and $0.7$, do they satisfy the basic weight condition?
options: Yes, they are nonnegative and sum to one
Yes, because weights can be any real numbers

questions.question: If $Z$ chooses group $1$ with probability $0.4$ and group $2$ with probability $0.6$, what are these probabilities in a mixture?
How is a mixture distribution related to the law of total probability?
options: It averages conditional distributions over cases of a random index
It uses only disjoint events with probability zero.
It applies only to deterministic functions

questions.question: Why can a mixture have several peaks?
options: Weights are allowed to be negative, for every possible choice of input.
Different components may concentrate probability around different values

questions.question: What is the role of the random index $Z$?
options: It selects which conditional component distribution applies
It is always equal to the observed value $X$
It forces the mixture weights to be negative
It removes the need for conditional distributions

questions.question: A mixture has component means $10$ and $20$ with weights $0.25$ and $0.75$. What weighted average expression gives the mixture mean when applicable?
If $70\%$ of customers are leisure customers and $30\%$ are business customers, what should the mixture weights sum to?
If $P(X\le x\mid Z=1)=0.2$, $P(Z=1)=0.4$, $P(X\le x\mid Z=2)=0.5$, and $P(Z=2)=0.6$, what is the mixture CDF value at $x$?
Why is a mixture not usually the same as choosing one component and ignoring the index probabilities?
options: The weights are irrelevant to the average
The index probabilities must all be equal
The overall distribution depends on how likely each component is
The components cannot be conditional distributions

questions.question: What would be invalid about mixture weights $0.8$ and $0.5$ for two components?
A population has two hidden groups with weights $0.9$ and $0.1$. Which group has greater influence on the mixture distribution?
Suppose each component score distribution is unimodal, but group means are far apart. What can happen to the mixture?
